extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists and educated public; researchers across natural sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Meeting reports, short research notes, experimental-method observations, and technical announcements published in a scientific journal issue; includes procedural details and instrument/identification claims useful for practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finger-print identification reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The finger-prints of any particular individual, from the youngest age to the most advanced, are invariable, and the concordance of the impressions of the ten digits would constitute practical certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The calculable chance of error for identification by concordance of ten digits is asserted to be less than one part in sixty-four billions; use concordant impressions of all ten digits to achieve 'practical certainty' in identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mecke blast burner operating pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Mecke blast burner (shown with and without the air-blast and with a water-blower), the pressure should be 2 kilos per sq. cm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified pressure (2 kilos per sq. cm.) for reproducible Mecke burner performance when photographing spectra or producing the chloride spectra described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographing chloride spectra exposure time
rubrics_metrics.description: For the production of chloride spectra (photographs shown of spectra of lime and calcium chloride), exposures of two hours were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long exposures (order of two hours) may be required to obtain clear photographic spectra of some salts with the described apparatus and burner arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spark-spectra pressure threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: When photographing the spark spectrum of metallic calcium in an atmosphere of hydrogen, at pressures less than 5 mm there was no distinct passage of the spark between the electrodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain pressures above about 5 mm to obtain a distinct spark passage; expect different electrode glow/scintillation phenomena at very low pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermal stability as diagnostic for yeast glucases (amygdalase vs maltase)
rubrics_metrics.description: True maltase could be destroyed by heating at 50°C, whilst activity towards amygdalin (amygdalase) was unimpaired; at high temperature (60°C) amygdalase is quickly destroyed leaving invertase active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differential heat inactivation (e.g., heating to 50°C) and extraction-temperature profiles (amygdalase extracted equally well at 15°–45°) as diagnostic criteria to distinguish specific yeast enzymes (maltase, amygdalase, invertase); note that zymogen activation by brief heating (e.g., 45°C) is reported for amygdalase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraction and zymogen activation conditions for yeast amygdalase
rubrics_metrics.description: Amygdalase is present in yeast as a 'symogen' or complex protein molecule that can be dissolved out at 0°C and have its hydrolytic activity developed by heating the solution for a short time at 45°C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To extract and activate amygdalase: dissolve zymogen at ~0°C, then briefly heat the extract at ~45°C to develop activity; note amygdalase resists autolysis and may be precipitated with invertase by alcohol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of chloride displacement by precipitants
rubrics_metrics.description: Sodium and potassium chlorides in saturated solutions exist in an easily precipitable, slightly hydrated form and pass into a more soluble and more hydrated form as the amount of precipitant (alcohol or hydrogen chloride) is increased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using alcohol or hydrogen chloride as precipitants, expect increasing precipitant to change the hydration/solubility state of salts; alcohol has less dehydrating power than hydrogen chloride though otherwise they act similarly as chloride precipitants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for assessing average concentrating (hydration) effect of salts
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the average concentrating effect of salts by hydrolysing cane sugar with nitric acid in their presence and ascertaining the extent to which the solution must be diluted to reduce the rate of change to the value when the salt is not present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the dilution required to restore the baseline hydrolysis rate (no-salt condition) as a metric of a salt's average degree of hydration/concentrating effect; this method was applied to nitrates to deduce degrees of hydration for various salts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of hydrolysis-based method to other substrates
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain whether the method (used for cane sugar hydrolysis) can be applied to other hydrolytes, the investigation was extended to the hydrolysis of methylic acetate by chlorhydric acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hydrolysis+rate/dilution approach can be tested on other substrates (e.g., methylic acetate) to evaluate whether salts exert similar concentrating/hydration effects across different hydrolytic reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental and sample-preparation recommendations for spectra work
rubrics_metrics.description: Use infusible supports instead of platinum in high-temperature flames (e.g., carborundum points, quartz fibres); for solutions use quartz tubes with a capillary orifice; for chloride spectra a by-pass carrying gas through chloroform-saturated sponge was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose chemically and thermally inert supports (carborundum, quartz) and appropriate sample-holding (capillary quartz tubes) to reduce contamination and obtain reproducible spectra; consider gas-supply modifications (chloroform by-pass) for chloride spectra production.
